items.title: AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos
items.summary: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. items.summary: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. items.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, but prompt transformations designed to preserve the underlying request can redistribute activity across them. items.title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization
items.summary: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. items.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. items.summary: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. items.title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation
items.summary: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. items.summary: An agent that truly knows and acts on behalf of its user has been a long-standing promise of AI assistants. items.summary: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. items.title: Rethinking Video Storage for AI Training: Breaking Cross-Frame Dependencies for Efficient Random Access
items.summary: Large-scale AI training increasingly relies on massive video datasets with random temporal sampling patterns. However, existing video storage paradigms are optimized for sequential playback and employ sophisticated inter-frame reference structures to maximize compression efficiency. items.summary: Recent test-time training (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. items.title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
items.summary: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. items.title: ReGE: Stronger Agents through Experience Synthesis
items.summary: Repeated attempts at interactive tasks uncover facts, useful operations, and failures that can inform subsequent execution. We introduce ReGE, a framework for turning this recorded experience into guidance for a fresh attempt. items.summary: Long-video generators increasingly retrieve past visual observations to prevent identity drift. items.summary: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. items.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. items.summary: Hallucination detection is increasingly important for evaluating and deploying large language models. items.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. items.summary: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately.
